Safe Lab Walkthrough — nine steps for every course, two more for the hard ones

A visual companion to the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy v2.0. Everything on this page turns a rule from that document into something you do at the keyboard, before you touch a tool. Steps 1 to 9 apply in all eight courses of the program. Steps 10 and 11 apply once you reach scanning, intrusion testing and malware handling. Compiled 13 September 2026.

The one rule underneath all of them. You may apply what you learn only to systems you own, or that you have written permission to work on. Your enrolment authorizes nothing. Your instructor cannot authorize you on a system he does not own. Unauthorized access, interception, scanning, exploitation and data interference are criminal offences in Canada — sections 342.1, 342.2, 430(1.1) and 184 of the Criminal Code — carrying up to ten years of imprisonment, and they end cybersecurity careers before they start.

The program is a ladder. In Term 1 you observe a network. Later you scan it, test it, and handle live malicious code and real incident data. The authorization rule never changes; what changes is how much written authorization you need first, and how much damage a mistake does. Section 7 of the Notice sets out what each course adds — read the part that applies to you before its first lab.

The animations below are schematic drawings, not screenshots. That is deliberate: no vendor's interface is reproduced here, and a diagram of the idea stays correct when the interface changes. Where a real product is involved, a dated note under the step says what was current when this page was written and what is likely to look different on your screen.

The eleven steps

  1. Read it, then sign it — once for every course
  2. Isolate the lab before you build it
  3. Snapshot before, restore after
  4. Check the link before you click it
  5. Verify the file, then install it
  6. The thirty-second authorization test
  7. Capture only what is yours
  8. If you stumble onto something real: stop
  9. What you hand in contains no real data
  10. Nothing is in scope until it is written down
  11. A live sample never leaves the box
1

Read it, then sign it — once for every course

Annex A is not paperwork. It is the record that you were told, in writing, what you may and may not do in this particular course — and it is the first thing anyone will ask for if a question is ever raised.

Do

  • Read all twenty-one sections, and read the part of section 7 that applies to this course.
  • Sign Annex A with your full name, student number and the date, and initial the section 7 lines your instructor identifies.
  • Hand it in at the first class and keep your own copy.

Do not

  • Assume the signature you gave last term covers this course — it does not.
  • Start any lab, download or installation before it is handed in.

Rules this comes from Annex A · §2.2 (acceptance) · §7 (what your course adds) · §9 (code of ethics)

2

Isolate the lab before you build it

Every rule that follows depends on this one being true. A lab attached to a real network is no longer a lab — it is activity on somebody else's system. This holds in all eight courses.

Do

  • Set the adapter to Host-only or Internal Network before first boot.
  • Keep the lab on the address range the lab guide gives you.
  • If a tool must be downloaded, fetch it on the host, verify it (Step 5), then move it into the VM.

Do not

  • Use a bridged adapter on campus, at home or on a café network.
  • Bridge a lab VM to an employer's network, "only for a minute".
  • Point any scan, capture or test at an address outside the lab range.

Rules this comes from §6.4 (lab rules) · §1.1 (Authorized Lab Environment, Designated Target) · §6.3

If your screen does not look like this

Checked 13 Sept 2026: Oracle VirtualBox 7.2.16 (released 18 Aug 2026) is the current stable build, and the setting is at Machine ▸ Settings ▸ Network ▸ Adapter 1 ▸ Attached to. Oracle ships maintenance releases every few weeks, so your build number will be higher and menu wording may shift. Other hypervisors name the same idea differently: VMware uses Host-only or a custom VMnet, Hyper-V uses an Internal or Private virtual switch, UTM and Parallels use their own labels. The principle — no path from the lab to a real network — is what you are marked on, not the menu path.

3

Snapshot before, restore after

Captures fill disks, scans crash services, hardening locks you out and samples destroy the machine they run on. A snapshot turns an evening of rebuilding into twenty seconds.

Do

  • Snapshot after the clean install, and again after the configuration is built.
  • Give snapshots names you will still understand in three weeks.
  • Back up host data too — the host is not protected by a VM snapshot.

Do not

  • Keep the only copy of your report inside the VM you are about to break.
  • Assume "I will be careful" is a recovery plan.

Rules this comes from §6.4 (snapshot and back up) · §10.3 (assumption of risk) · §10.4 (your equipment)

If your screen does not look like this

Checked 13 Sept 2026: the feature is called Snapshots in VirtualBox, Snapshot Manager in VMware Workstation and Fusion, and Checkpoints in Hyper-V. On rented cloud infrastructure the equivalent is an image or volume snapshot, and it is usually billed — check the provider's pricing before leaving snapshots lying around.

4

Check the link before you click it

Course links, vendor mirrors and repositories all go stale. Domains expire and get re-registered by someone else; mirrors get tampered with. Checking costs ten seconds.

Do

  • Paste the link into a multi-engine reputation service before opening it — virustotal.com/gui/home/url.
  • Cross-check the domain at Google Safe Browsing site status.
  • Read the domain letter by letter, and prefer the publisher's own site over any mirror.
  • Tell your instructor about any broken or suspicious link in the course material.

Do not

  • Treat a clean verdict as proof of safety — new malicious pages are clean for hours.
  • Upload files containing confidential or personal data to a public scanner: submissions become visible to other subscribers of the service.
  • Open a shortened link without expanding it first.

Rules this comes from §14 (external links and downloads) · Annex C (link and download checklist)

If your screen does not look like this

Checked 13 Sept 2026: VirusTotal rolled out URL Scanning 2.0 during July and August 2026. URL reports now include full-browser telemetry — page screenshots, the rendered DOM, network request logs — and a history timeline showing how a page changed over time. The report page therefore looks noticeably different from screenshots in tutorials written before mid-2026, and some panels depend on account tier. The address is unchanged and the headline number — how many engines flagged it — is still the thing you need. Engine counts move as vendors come and go, so "94" is an example, not a fixed figure.

5

Verify the file, then install it

A publisher tells you what its file should look like, down to the last character. If your copy differs, it is not their file — whatever the download page said.

Do

  • Windows PowerShell: Get-FileHash .\file.exe -Algorithm SHA256
  • Windows cmd: certutil -hashfile file.exe SHA256
  • Linux: sha256sum file.iso — macOS: shasum -a 256 file.iso
  • Compare against the hash on the publisher's own page, not one on the mirror you downloaded from.

Do not

  • Run an installer whose hash does not match, "to see if it works".
  • Use cracked, patched or unlicensed software, or bypass a trial limit — a separate offence and a separate breach of the course rules.

Rules this comes from §14.2 (verify before you run) · §6.6 (software licences) · Annex C

6

The thirty-second authorization test

This is the single rule that separates a cybersecurity technician from a defendant, and it is identical in all eight courses. Run it before every scan, capture, install, test or login.

Do

  • Get permission in writing, naming the systems, the purpose and the dates — Annex D is a template you can hand to an owner.
  • Stay inside the scope: those hosts, that window, that purpose.
  • Ask your instructor first when a situation is not covered by the lab guide.

Do not

  • Accept "sure, go ahead" from a friend for a network their employer owns — they cannot give it.
  • Assume that being enrolled in a cybersecurity program authorizes anything at all.
  • Rely on "I did no damage" or "I only looked" — neither is a defence.

Rules this comes from §6.1 (authorization) · §8.2 (Criminal Code) · Annex D (written authorization template)

7

Capture only what is yours

Packet capture runs through most of the program and is the fastest way to commit an offence by accident. On a shared network, the traffic you record belongs to other people.

Do

  • Capture on the lab interface, filtered to the lab addresses.
  • Keep only what your report needs, and delete the rest when the exercise is marked.
  • Treat anything personal you see by accident as confidential — and say nothing about it.

Do not

  • Enable promiscuous or monitor mode on home, residence, campus, workplace or public Wi-Fi.
  • Capture "just to practise" at work, even on a network you administer, without written authorization.
  • Keep or share a capture containing real personal data, credentials or internal addresses.

Rules this comes from §6.3 · §6.7 (data and privacy in labs) · §7.2 (monitoring and capture) · §8.2 (s. 184) · §8.3 (privacy law)

If your screen does not look like this

Checked 13 Sept 2026: Wireshark 4.6.8 and the 4.4.18 maintenance release both came out on 12 Aug 2026, and a 4.7.x development line is running toward a future 5.0 — expect menus and dialogue names to move when that lands. Capture privileges are configured differently on each platform (Npcap on Windows, the wireshark group and dumpcap capabilities on Linux, ChmodBPF on macOS), so follow the setup in your lab guide rather than a video made for another OS.

8

If you stumble onto something real: stop

Sooner or later something outside the lab will look wrong — an exposed share, an open console, a password in a log, a host that answers when it should not. What you do next decides how this ends.

Do

  • Stop at once and close what you opened.
  • Write down only what you already saw: date, time, address, what appeared.
  • Report it the same day to the system owner or the College IT service, and tell your instructor.

Do not

  • Test whether it can be exploited "to confirm the finding".
  • Download, copy or screenshot the data you found.
  • Post it, message it to classmates, or mention it publicly before it is fixed.

Rules this comes from §6.8 (accidental discovery) · §7.7.5 (out of scope during a test) · §9 item 6 (disclose responsibly)

9

What you hand in contains no real data

A submitted report is copied, marked, stored and backed up. You do not get it back. Anything real in it is a privacy breach with your name on the cover page.

Do

  • Use the fictional organization, users and addresses given for the exercise.
  • Check screenshots for hostnames, IPs, e-mail addresses and browser tabs before pasting them in.
  • Say "not captured — fictional lab data" where a credential would otherwise appear.

Do not

  • Include real addresses, real names, real credentials or an employer's internal data.
  • Substitute a real organization for the fictional one "to make it more realistic".
  • Share lab credentials, VM images, samples, scope documents, quizzes or solutions with anyone.

Rules this comes from §6.7 · §18.2 (submitted work) · §17.2 (confidentiality) · §8.3 (privacy law, including Law 25)

Two more, once you reach the higher-risk courses

These do not replace anything above. They are what gets added when a course moves from watching a system to probing it, or from reading about malicious code to running it.

10

Nothing is in scope until it is written down

Applies to 420-3C1-DW Managing Vulnerabilities · 420-3C2-DW Intrusion Test — and any work on a real organization

A scan is an intrusive act, not an observation, and an exploit leaves proof of what you did on the target. From this point in the program, the written scope is the only thing standing between an exercise and an offence.

Do

  • Before any scan or test, have the scope in front of you: targets, exclusions, permitted techniques, time window, who to call if something breaks. For labs, the lab guide is that document.
  • Check every address against it, including ones you found by pivoting.
  • For anything outside the lab, use Annex D and get it signed by someone entitled to sign it.
  • Leave nothing behind: no accounts, no implants, no persistence, no artefacts.

Do not

  • Scan or test a host because it answered, because it was in the same subnet, or because it looked unused.
  • Treat a bug-bounty target or a public CTF as though the course authorized it — that is your own private activity under someone else's rules.
  • Run denial-of-service, stress or flood testing unless an exercise expressly instructs it inside the lab.
  • Reuse credentials, hashes or shells obtained in an exercise anywhere else.

Rules this comes from §7.6 (vulnerability scanning) · §7.7 (intrusion testing) · §7.7.5 · Annex D

11

A live sample never leaves the box

Applies to 420-1C2-DW Threats and Risks · 420-4C1-DW Incident Management

Handling live malicious code is ordinary professional work, done in an environment built for it. Moving that code anywhere else — even by accident, even to be helpful — is distributing malware.

Do

  • Run samples only in the analysis environment designated for that exercise, snapshotted, with networking disabled or host-only.
  • Turn off shared folders, shared clipboard and drag-and-drop before the sample exists.
  • Restore the snapshot when the exercise ends, and confirm the sample is gone.
  • Preserve evidence properly: work on copies, record hashes and times, do not alter originals.

Do not

  • Execute a sample on a host OS, a personal device, a phone, or any employer equipment.
  • E-mail, message, sync, upload or hand a sample to anyone, including a classmate.
  • Upload confidential samples to public multi-engine services — subscribers can download them.
  • Visit live malicious infrastructure or contact a threat actor to "investigate".

Rules this comes from §7.3 (threat information and samples) · §7.8 (incident response and malware handling) · §17.2

What changes course by course

The same nine steps run through every course. This is the extra rule each one brings with it, and the mistake students most often make in it. Full text in section 7 and Annex E of the Notice.

420-1C1-DW75 h · Term 1

Preventative Monitoring

Capture on designated targets inside the lab, never on a shared network.

Most common mistake Running a capture on home or campus Wi-Fi to get "real traffic".

§7.2

420-1C2-DW75 h · Term 1

Threats and Risks

Study threat information; never interact with live malicious infrastructure or its operators.

Most common mistake Opening a phishing or C2 link from a personal machine, or downloading a breach dump.

§7.3

420-2C1-DW90 h · Term 1

Cyber Defense

A defensive change is still a change: owner's written approval, a window, and a rollback.

Most common mistake Applying a hardening baseline or firewall rule to a live system and cutting off its users.

§7.2 · §7.4

420-2C2-DW45 h · Term 2

Compliance Assessments

No real organization's documents without written permission; every finding is confidential.

Most common mistake Using an employer's real policies or gap analysis as the case study.

§7.5

420-3C1-DW60 h · Term 2

Managing Vulnerabilities

Scan only the designated range — a scan is intrusive and is logged as an attack.

Most common mistake A "quick sweep" of the local subnet, the residence network or a cloud target.

§7.6

420-3C2-DW90 h · Term 2

Intrusion Test

Nothing is in scope until a written scope document names it. Leave nothing behind.

Most common mistake Treating a reachable host, a bounty target or a public CTF as course-authorized.

§7.7

420-4C1-DW75 h · Term 2

Incident Management

Samples run only in the designated isolated environment and never leave it.

Most common mistake Detonating a sample on the host OS, or sending one to a classmate.

§7.3 · §7.8

420-4C2-DW60 h · Term 3

Implementation and Management of Corporate Cybersecurity Measures

Written authorization before anything real; the employer's rules take precedence.

Most common mistake Implementing a course design on a real network without authorization from the right person.

§7.4 · §7.5 · §7.9

The sixty-second check, before every lab

Print this page, or run the list from memory. Two of these apply only to some courses — you will know which.

  • Annex A signed and handed in for this course.
  • Section 7 read for this course — I know what it adds.
  • VM adapter set to Host-only or Internal — verified, not assumed.
  • Snapshot taken and named.
  • Every link scanned; every download hash-checked against the publisher's page.
  • Authorization test passed for every target I intend to touch.
  • Scope document in front of me, if this course scans or tests.
  • Analysis VM sealed — networking, shared folders and clipboard off — if this course handles samples.
  • Capture filter limited to lab addresses.
  • Host data backed up; enough free disk for the exercise.
  • Fictional data only in anything I will submit.

Scope of this page

This walkthrough is teaching material, not legal advice, and it does not replace the Legal Notice, the laboratory guides and scope documents, or Dawson College's Institutional Student Evaluation Policy, Student Code of Conduct and IT resource rules — all of which continue to apply in full. Where this page and any of those documents differ, the stricter rule governs what you do.
